final_text:
I have enough evidence to compile the report. No SHA256 of a transferred file could be extracted since the payload delivery itself occurred over TLS (not observable), and the C2 protocol traffic is application-layer encrypted (not TLS, but obfuscated NetSupport RAT payload) — no plaintext executable was transferred in the clear in this capture.

---

# Incident Report: NetSupport RAT Infection — MTA-2026-02-28

## 1. Victim Host

| Attribute | Value |
|---|---|
| IPv4 address | **10.2.28.88** |
| MAC address | **00:19:d1:b2:4d:ad** (Intel NIC) |
| Windows hostname | **DESKTOP-TEYQ2NR** |
| Windows workgroup/domain | EASYAS123 (domain: easyas123.tech) |
| Logged-in Windows user | **brolf** (observed as Kerberos CNameString from 10.2.28.88 to DC at 10.2.28.2) |
| OS fingerprint | Windows 10/11 (Chrome/Edge 145.0.0.0 user-agent, DHCP hostname DESKTOP-TEYQ2NR) |

DHCP lease confirms 10.2.28.88 was assigned to host DESKTOP-TEYQ2NR (MAC 00:19:d1:b2:4d:ad) by the gateway 10.2.28.1. NBNS/browser announcements confirm the same host/workgroup pairing.

## 2. Malware Family

**NetSupport RAT** (malicious deployment of the legitimate NetSupport Manager remote-control client) — **signature-confirmed**.

Evidence:
- HTTP `User-Agent: NetSupport Manager/1.3` on all outbound C2 POST requests.
- Requests to the literal path `/fakeurl.htm`, which is the fixed check-in endpoint used by the NetSupport Manager client/gateway protocol.
- Application-layer protocol fields consistent with the NetSupport client-to-gateway protocol: client sends `CMD=ENCD` / `ES=1` / `DATA=<encrypted blob>`, server (attacker infrastructure) responds `CMD=POLL` / `INFO=1` / `ACK=1`.
- Beaconing is highly regular (~60-second interval) for over 4.3 hours (23:55:51 to 04:16:28, 264 POST requests observed), consistent with an active remote-control/backdoor session rather than benign traffic.

## 3. Indicators of Compromise

### Command-and-Control
| Type | Value |
|---|---|
| C2 domain | **vadusa.xyz** |
| C2 IP:port | **45.131.214.85:443** (plaintext HTTP carried over TCP/443, not TLS) |
| C2 URL (beacon endpoint) | **http://45.131.214.85/fakeurl.htm** (POST, `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`) |
| Beacon interval | ~60 seconds, 264 requests logged 2026-02-28 23:55:51 → 2026-03-01 04:16:28 |
| Client User-Agent | `NetSupport Manager/1.3` |

### Likely infection vector (behavioral, not signature-confirmed)
- 10.2.28.88 made a TLS connection to **www.fmcsa.dot.gov** (23.64.147.24) at 23:55:50.96.
- Within the same second, the host performed a DNS lookup for **vadusa.xyz**, which resolved to 45.131.214.85 at 23:55:51.37.
- The first NetSupport RAT beacon fired 20 ms later, at 23:55:51.39.

This tight timing chain (legitimate-site TLS session → immediate lookup of the attacker domain → immediate RAT check-in) indicates the fmcsa.dot.gov page load led directly to execution of the RAT, consistent with the known "fake CAPTCHA/verification" (ClickFix-style) delivery pattern used in NetSupport RAT campaigns. This portion is **behavioral inference**, not a directly observed file drop — the pcap does not contain a plaintext executable download, so no dropped file name or SHA256 hash could be recovered from this capture.

### File names / hashes
None recoverable. All malware delivery and C2 traffic in this capture is either TLS-encrypted (the fmcsa.dot.gov session) or carried as an opaque encrypted blob inside the NetSupport RAT's own protocol (`DATA=` field in the `/fakeurl.htm` exchanges); no binary object with computable SHA256 was transferred in the clear.

## 4. Summary

DESKTOP-TEYQ2NR (10.2.28.88, MAC 00:19:d1:b2:4d:ad, user "brolf") was compromised with **NetSupport RAT**. Infection appears to have followed a browser session to a spoofed/compromised FMCSA-themed page, after which the host began resolving and beaconing to the attacker-controlled domain **vadusa.xyz (45.131.214.85)** over port 443 using the NetSupport client protocol against **/fakeurl.htm**. The RAT maintained an active check-in channel for over 4 hours at the time the capture ends, with no evidence of remediation in this capture window. All other DNS/HTTP/TLS activity observed (Windows Update, OCSP/DigiCert, Microsoft telemetry, MSN, Bing, Office, Adobe, Skype, Nvidia GFE, Google Update) is normal enterprise/background traffic and not indicative of compromise.
